decks.title: Locomotion and Movement, Part 1: Muscles and how they contract
goals: Distinguish ciliary, flagellar and muscular movement, and compare red and white muscle fibres
Describe the organisation of skeletal muscle, draw and label a sarcomere, and name the contractile proteins
Explain the sliding filament theory, the role of calcium and ATP, summation, tetanus and rigor mortis

slides.heading: Movement and muscle
slides.body_md: Part 1: how cells and muscles move, and how a sarcomere shortens.

visual.alt: Movement divided into ciliary, flagellar and muscular movement

slides.narration: Movement is a basic property of living things. Some cells move by tiny hairs or whips, but most of the movement we see in animals is made by muscles pulling on bones.

slides.heading: Types of movement
slides.body_md: All **locomotion** (moving from place to place) is movement, but not every movement is locomotion.

rows: Cilia beating together in one direction
Dust and mucus swept up the windpipe; ovum pushed along the oviduct
A sperm swimming; Euglena in a pond

visual.alt: Table of ciliary, flagellar and muscular movement

slides.narration: Cilia are short and beat in waves like a field of grass in wind. A flagellum is long and drives the whole cell forward. Muscular movement is the most important for human locomotion.

slides.heading: Muscle: properties and kinds
slides.body_md: Muscle tissue has four general properties: **excitability** (responds to a stimulus), **contractility** (shortens), **extensibility** (can be stretched) and **elasticity** (returns to its length).

visual.alt: Table comparing skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle

slides.narration: Muscle can be stimulated, can shorten, can be stretched and then springs back. The three kinds differ in appearance, in control and in where they are found.

slides.heading: Red and white muscle fibres
slides.body_md: Skeletal muscle fibres differ in how they make ATP.

rows: Leg muscles of a hen; muscles of diving seals

visual.alt: Table comparing red and white muscle fibres

slides.narration: Red fibres are packed with the oxygen-storing pigment myoglobin and with mitochondria, so they work for long periods. White fibres rely on a quick but short-lived supply of energy, so they give short bursts and tire.

slides.heading: Organisation of a skeletal muscle
slides.body_md: A muscle is built from ever smaller parts. Each fibre is a long cell with many nuclei, covered by the **sarcolemma**, with cytoplasm called **sarcoplasm** and a store of calcium, the **sarcoplasmic reticulum**.

visual.alt: Flow from muscle to bundles, fibre, myofibrils and myofilaments

slides.narration: A whole muscle contains bundles of fibres. Each fibre holds many myofibrils, and each myofibril is made of two kinds of protein filament, thin actin and thick myosin, lying side by side.

slides.heading: The sarcomere
slides.body_md: A **sarcomere** lies between two **Z lines**. The **A band** (dark) is the length of the thick filaments; the **I band** (light) has only thin filaments and is cut by the Z line; the **H zone** is the middle of the A band with no thin filaments; the **M line** holds the thick filaments together.

slides.narration: The dark A band and the light I band give the muscle its striped look. When the sarcomere is relaxed, the thin filaments stop short of each other in the middle, leaving the H zone.

slides.heading: Contractile proteins
slides.body_md: **Thin filament:** two strands of **actin**, a thread of **tropomyosin** in the groove, and **troponin** at intervals. **Thick filament:** many **myosin** molecules; each has a tail and a double head whose **ATPase** site splits ATP and which binds actin.

visual.alt: A thin filament with actin, tropomyosin and troponin, and a myosin molecule with head and tail

slides.narration: Tropomyosin lies over the places on actin where myosin can bind, and troponin holds it there. The myosin head can attach to actin and also splits adenosine triphosphate to release energy.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: bands of a sarcomere
slides.body_md: In a model muscle, the A band is 1.5 µm and each thin filament is 1 µm long. Find the total I band and the H zone when the sarcomere is 2.8 µm long, and again when it is 2.2 µm.
bullets: Relaxed: I band $= 2.8 - 1.5 = 1.3\ \mu\text{m}$; each half $= 0.65$. Thin filament inside the A band, each side $= 1 - 0.65 = 0.35$. H zone $= 1.5 - 2 \times 0.35 = 0.8\ \mu\text{m}$.
Contracted: I band $= 2.2 - 1.5 = 0.7$; overlap $= 1 - 0.35 = 0.65$; H zone $= 1.5 - 2 \times 0.65 = 0.2\ \mu\text{m}$.
The A band stays 1.5 µm; only the I band and H zone narrow.

visual.alt: Worked table: H zone 0.8 falls to 0.2, A band constant

slides.narration: Subtract the A band from the sarcomere length to get the whole light band. Each thin filament then reaches further into the dark band as the light band shrinks, and the middle gap becomes narrower. The dark band does not change.

slides.heading: Quick check: H zone
slides.body_md: Find the H zone at a given sarcomere length.
slides.narration: Quick check. Use the same method with a shorter sarcomere.

slides.heading: Neuromuscular junction and calcium
slides.body_md: A motor neuron meets a fibre at the **motor end plate**. In a resting fibre, tropomyosin covers the myosin-binding sites on actin.

nodes.label: Nerve impulse reaches the motor end plate
Acetylcholine released; action potential in the sarcolemma
Calcium binds troponin; tropomyosin moves aside

visual.alt: Flow from nerve impulse to exposure of myosin-binding sites

slides.narration: The nerve releases acetylcholine, which sets off an electrical signal along the muscle membrane. Calcium floods out of its store, binds troponin, and uncovers the sites on actin where myosin can grip.

slides.heading: Cross-bridge cycle and the sliding filaments
slides.body_md: Each myosin head repeats a four-step cycle, pulling the thin filaments towards the M line. This is the **sliding filament theory** of Huxley and Huxley.

nodes.label: Head with ADP and phosphate binds actin: cross bridge
Power stroke: head bends, thin filament slides
New ATP binds: head lets go

visual.alt: Cycle of attach, power stroke, detach and recock

slides.narration: The myosin head attaches, bends and drags the thin filament inward, then a fresh molecule of adenosine triphosphate binds and the head lets go. Splitting that molecule resets the head, ready to attach again further along.

slides.heading: Quick check: calcium
slides.body_md: Predict what happens when calcium binding to troponin is blocked.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about what tropomyosin does when calcium is absent.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: shortening of a fibre
slides.body_md: A muscle fibre 4.2 cm long is made of sarcomeres of 2.8 µm joined end to end. When it contracts, every sarcomere shortens to 2.2 µm. How many sarcomeres are in the fibre, and by how much does it shorten?
bullets: Each shortens by $2.8 - 2.2 = 0.6\ \mu\text{m}$, so the fibre shortens by $15000 \times 0.6 = 9000\ \mu\text{m} = 9$ mm.
Each sarcomere shortens by 21.4 percent, so the fibre does too.

visual.alt: Worked table: 15000 sarcomeres, 9 millimetres

slides.narration: Count the sarcomeres by dividing the fibre length by the length of one. Each one shortens by the same small amount, and because they are all in a line the tiny changes add up to a visible shortening.

slides.heading: Twitch, summation and tetanus
slides.body_md: A single stimulus gives a **twitch**. If the next stimulus comes before relaxation is complete, the contractions add up: **summation**. At a very high rate the muscle stays smoothly contracted: **tetanus**.

visual.alt: Tension recordings showing a single twitch, summation and tetanus

slides.narration: One stimulus gives one short twitch. If stimuli arrive before the muscle has relaxed, each twitch builds on the last and tension climbs. At a very high rate the twitches fuse into a steady, strong contraction called tetanus.

slides.heading: Stimulation rate and rigor mortis
slides.body_md: In the model, a twitch lasts 120 ms and its contraction phase 40 ms. The response depends on the interval between stimuli.

rows: Rigor mortis: heads stay locked on actin

visual.alt: Table of stimulation rate, interval and response, with rigor mortis

slides.narration: The faster the stimuli come, the less time the muscle has to relax. After death no new adenosine triphosphate is made, so myosin heads cannot let go of actin and the body becomes stiff. This is rigor mortis.

slides.heading: Quick check: stimulation rate
slides.body_md: Work out the time between stimuli at a given rate.
slides.narration: Quick check. Divide one thousand milliseconds by the number of stimuli.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Movement: ciliary, flagellar, muscular; muscle properties are excitability, contractility, extensibility, elasticity.
Red fibres: myoglobin, mitochondria, aerobic, slow; white fibres: few mitochondria, glycolysis, fast, tire.
Sarcomere: Z to Z; A band constant, I band and H zone narrow on contraction.
Calcium binds troponin, tropomyosin moves, myosin heads cycle using ATP, thin filaments slide.
Summation and tetanus come from rapid stimuli; rigor mortis is lack of ATP.

visual.alt: Summary table of sarcomere changes

slides.narration: To recap: muscle contraction is the sliding of thin filaments over thick ones. Calcium switches it on, adenosine triphosphate powers each cycle, and the dark band stays the same while the light band and the middle gap shrink.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Label a sarcomere with **Z line, A band, I band, H zone and M line**.
State that the **A band does not change** during contraction.
Name the proteins and their positions: **actin, tropomyosin, troponin, myosin**.
Write the steps in order: impulse, acetylcholine, calcium, cross bridge, power stroke, ATP.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Label every band of the sarcomere. Remember that the dark band never changes length. Name each protein with its position. And give the steps of contraction in the right order.

goals: List the bones of the axial and appendicular skeleton with their numbers, and state the functions of the skeleton
Classify joints as fibrous, cartilaginous or synovial and give an example of each synovial type

slides.heading: The skeleton and its joints
slides.body_md: Part 2: bones, joints, and what goes wrong with them.

visual.alt: Skeleton divided into axial and appendicular parts, with joints

slides.narration: The skeleton gives the body its shape and works with muscles to produce movement. In this part we count the bones, classify the joints between them and study the commonest disorders.

slides.heading: Functions of the skeleton
slides.body_md: The skeleton does much more than hold us up.

rows: The vertebral column holds the trunk upright
Skull guards the brain; rib cage guards heart and lungs
Bones act as levers pulled by muscles
Red bone marrow makes blood cells
Calcium and phosphate; fat in yellow marrow

visual.alt: Table of functions of the skeleton

slides.narration: Bones support the body, protect delicate organs and act as levers for muscles. The red marrow makes blood cells, and the bone itself stores calcium and phosphate.

slides.heading: The adult skeleton in numbers
slides.body_md: The adult skeleton has **206 bones**: the **axial skeleton** (80) forms the main axis of the body, and the **appendicular skeleton** (126) includes the limbs and their girdles.

slides.narration: The axial skeleton is the skull, backbone, breastbone and ribs. The appendicular skeleton is the shoulder and hip girdles with the arms and legs. Together they make two hundred and six bones.

slides.heading: Skull and vertebral column
slides.body_md: The skull has 29 bones in this count. The vertebral column has 26 bones in an adult, because 5 sacral and 4 coccygeal vertebrae of a child fuse.

rows: Ear ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes in each ear)

visual.alt: Table of skull and vertebral column bones

slides.narration: The skull is counted as cranium, face, the hyoid bone and the six tiny bones of the middle ears. In a child the lower end of the backbone has separate vertebrae, which later fuse into the sacrum and the coccyx.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: bones of the hands and feet
slides.body_md: How many bones are there in both hands and both feet together? What fraction of the whole skeleton is this?
bullets: One hand: carpals 8, metacarpals 5, phalanges 14: $8 + 5 + 14 = 27$.
One foot: tarsals 7, metatarsals 5, phalanges 14: $7 + 5 + 14 = 26$.
Both: $2 \times (27 + 26) = 106$, a little over half of the 206 bones.

visual.alt: Worked table: 106 bones in hands and feet

slides.narration: Count the wrist, palm and finger bones of one hand, then the ankle, foot and toe bones of one foot, and double the total. More than half of all the bones of the body are in the hands and feet.

slides.heading: Quick check: hyoid
slides.body_md: Name the bone that does not articulate with any other bone.
slides.narration: Quick check. It lies at the base of the tongue.

slides.heading: Ribs, girdles and limbs
slides.body_md: There are **24 ribs** in twelve pairs: seven **true** pairs join the sternum directly, three **false** pairs join through the cartilage above, and two **floating** pairs are free in front. Each limb has 30 bones in the arm and 30 in the leg.

rows: Pectoral girdle (clavicle and scapula, both sides)
Upper limbs (humerus, radius, ulna, 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges, each)
Lower limbs (femur, tibia, fibula, patella, 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges, each)

visual.alt: Table of the appendicular skeleton

slides.narration: Each hip bone is formed by three fused bones. The kneecap, or patella, has no partner in the arm. The shoulder girdle is made of the collar bone and shoulder blade on each side.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: adding up the skeleton
slides.body_md: Show that the axial and appendicular bones add up to the whole skeleton, and find how many vertebrae a young child has compared with an adult.
bullets: Child: $7 + 12 + 5 + 5 + 4 = 33$ vertebrae; adult 26.

visual.alt: Worked table: 80 plus 126 equals 206

slides.narration: Add the four axial groups, then the four appendicular groups, and then the two totals. A child has more vertebrae than an adult because the lowest ones are separate until they fuse.

slides.heading: Quick check: ribs
slides.body_md: Identify the type of rib from its attachment.
slides.narration: Quick check. Which ribs join the cartilage of the rib above?

slides.heading: Classification of joints
slides.body_md: A **joint** is where two bones meet. Joints are classified by what lies between the bones.

visual.alt: Table classifying joints as fibrous, cartilaginous and synovial

slides.narration: In fibrous joints the bones are fused together by fibres and do not move. Cartilaginous joints allow a little movement. Synovial joints have a fluid-filled space and allow the greatest freedom.

slides.heading: Types of synovial joint
slides.body_md: Synovial joints differ in the shape of the bone surfaces, and so in the movements they allow.

slides.heading: Disorders of muscle
slides.body_md: Three disorders affect muscle function.

rows: Autoimmune: antibodies attack acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction
Low calcium in body fluids (for example, low parathormone)
Genetic; progressive degeneration of skeletal muscle (Duchenne: X-linked, no dystrophin)

visual.alt: Table of muscle disorders: cause and symptom

slides.narration: In myasthenia gravis the body attacks its own receptors, so the signal from the nerve fails to reach the muscle. In tetany, low calcium makes nerves over-excitable, giving spasms. In muscular dystrophy the muscle fibres slowly break down.

slides.heading: Disorders of bone and joints
slides.body_md: Three disorders affect bones and joints.

rows: Inflammation of joints: wear of cartilage, or autoimmune attack on the synovial membrane
Decreased bone mass, common after menopause when oestrogen falls
Crystals of uric acid deposited in joints
Sudden, very painful swelling, often of the big toe

visual.alt: Table of bone and joint disorders: cause and symptom

slides.narration: Arthritis means swollen painful joints. In osteoporosis the bones become thin and break easily, especially in older women. In gout, uric acid crystals collect in a joint and cause sudden severe pain.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Adult skeleton: 206 bones; axial 80 and appendicular 126.
Skull 29, vertebral column 26, sternum 1, ribs 24; girdles and limbs make 126.
Joints: fibrous (fixed), cartilaginous (slight), synovial (free): ball and socket, hinge, pivot, gliding, saddle.
Muscle disorders: myasthenia gravis, tetany, muscular dystrophy.
Bone and joint disorders: arthritis, osteoporosis, gout.

notes.title: Locomotion and Movement — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Types of movement; muscle properties; red and white fibres
sections.body_md:
**Movement** is a basic property of living organisms; **locomotion** is movement from one place to another, so all locomotion is movement but not all movement is locomotion (a tentacle of *Hydra* waving is movement without locomotion). Three kinds of movement are studied in humans:
- **Ciliary movement:** coordinated beating of **cilia** in one direction. The ciliated epithelium of the trachea sweeps dust and mucus towards the throat; cilia of the oviduct and the ciliated cells of the fallopian tube help to move the ovum.
- **Flagellar movement:** a long **flagellum** drives the cell, as in a **sperm** or in *Euglena*.
- **Muscular movement:** **contraction of muscle fibres**, which moves limbs, jaws, the tongue and also the heart and gut.

**General properties of muscle:** **excitability** (responds to a stimulus), **contractility** (can shorten), **extensibility** (can be stretched) and **elasticity** (returns to its original length after stretching).

**Kinds of muscle:** **skeletal** (striated, voluntary, attached to bones), **smooth or visceral** (unstriated, involuntary, in walls of hollow organs) and **cardiac** (striated, branched, involuntary, in the heart).

**Red and white fibres of skeletal muscle**
| Feature | Red fibres | White fibres |
|---|---|---|
| Myoglobin | Abundant (look red) | Little (look pale) |
| Mitochondria | Many | Few |
| Sarcoplasmic reticulum | Less | More |
| ATP made by | Aerobic respiration | Anaerobic glycolysis (lactic acid) |
| Contraction | Slow, sustained, resists fatigue | Fast, powerful, fatigues quickly |
| Examples | Leg muscles of a hen; muscles of diving mammals such as seals | Breast muscles of a domestic hen; muscles of the eyeball |

*Note on books:* some books give only the first four rows; the contrast of breast (white) and leg (red) muscle of a hen is a common textbook illustration.

key_terms.definition_md: Movement of the whole body from one place to another.
Ability of muscle to respond to a stimulus.
Oxygen-storing pigment of muscle; abundant in red fibres.
Slow, aerobic, fatigue-resistant fibre rich in myoglobin and mitochondria.

sections.heading: 2a. Structure of skeletal muscle and the contractile proteins
sections.body_md:
A skeletal muscle is a bundle of **fascicles**; each fascicle contains many **muscle fibres**. A fibre is a long, multinucleate cell enclosed in the **sarcolemma**; its cytoplasm is the **sarcoplasm**, and its modified endoplasmic reticulum, the **sarcoplasmic reticulum**, stores **calcium ions**. A fibre contains many parallel **myofibrils**, each made of **myofilaments** of two kinds.

**Sarcomere:** the **functional unit of contraction**, the segment of a myofibril between two successive **Z lines**.
- **A band (anisotropic, dark):** the length of the **thick (myosin) filaments**; the central part of the A band with no thin filaments in a relaxed fibre is the **H zone**; the **M line** in its middle holds the thick filaments.
- **I band (isotropic, light):** only **thin (actin) filaments**; it is bisected by the **Z line**.

**Contractile proteins**
- **Actin:** the thin filament is a double helix of **F-actin**, each a polymer of globular **G-actin**; a thread of **tropomyosin** lies in the groove and a **troponin** complex sits at regular intervals.
- **Myosin:** the thick filament is a bundle of **myosin** molecules. Each has a rod-like **tail (light meromyosin)** and a double **head (heavy meromyosin)** that projects as a cross bridge; the head has an **ATPase** site and an **actin-binding site**.

In the chapter, a model sarcomere is used with an A band of 1.5 µm and thin filaments 1 µm long; book values differ slightly (the A band is usually about 1.5 to 1.6 µm), so the arithmetic is illustrative.

key_terms.definition_md: Unit of contraction between two Z lines.
Dark band formed by thick filaments; length unchanged in contraction.
Light band of thin filaments only; bisected by the Z line.
Middle of the A band without thin filaments.
Thread that covers the myosin-binding sites on actin in a resting muscle.

sections.heading: 2b. Sliding filament theory, summation, tetanus and rigor mortis
sections.body_md:
**Sliding filament theory (Huxley and Huxley, 1954):** during contraction the **thin filaments slide inwards over the thick filaments** towards the M line; the filaments themselves do not shorten.

**Chemical events**
1. A nerve impulse reaches the **motor end plate**; **acetylcholine** is released and sets up an **action potential in the sarcolemma**.
2. The **sarcoplasmic reticulum** releases **calcium ions** into the sarcoplasm.
3. Calcium **binds troponin**; **tropomyosin** moves aside and uncovers the **myosin-binding sites** on actin.
4. A myosin head carrying **ADP and phosphate** binds actin: a **cross bridge**.
5. **Power stroke:** the head bends, releasing ADP and phosphate and pulling the thin filament towards the M line.
6. A fresh **ATP** binds the head, which **detaches**; ATP is split, which **recocks** the head. The cycle repeats while calcium is present.
7. **Relaxation:** calcium is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum; tropomyosin covers the sites again and the muscle returns to its resting length.

**Effect on the sarcomere:** the **Z lines come closer**; the **I band** and **H zone** narrow (the H zone may disappear); the **A band keeps its length**. With the model values, a sarcomere of 2.8 µm has an I band of 1.3 µm and an H zone of 0.8 µm; at 2.2 µm they are 0.7 µm and 0.2 µm.

**Twitch, summation, tetanus:** a single stimulus gives a **twitch**. If a second stimulus arrives before the muscle has relaxed, the contractions **add up** (**summation**). At a high rate of stimulation the contractions fuse into a smooth, sustained, stronger contraction: **tetanus**. (Model: twitch 120 ms, contraction 40 ms; the boundaries are illustrative.)

**Rigor mortis:** after death **ATP is no longer made**, so myosin heads **cannot detach** from actin and the muscles stay stiff; it sets in a few hours after death and passes off after a day or two, when the muscle proteins break down.

sections.heading: 3. The human skeleton
sections.body_md:
The adult skeleton has **206 bones**: **axial skeleton 80** and **appendicular skeleton 126**.

**Axial skeleton (80):**
- **Skull 29:** cranium **8** (frontal 1, parietal 2, temporal 2, occipital 1, sphenoid 1, ethmoid 1), face **14** (maxillae 2, zygomatic 2, nasal 2, lacrimal 2, palatine 2, inferior nasal conchae 2, vomer 1, mandible 1), **hyoid** 1, and **ear ossicles** 6 (malleus, incus, stapes in each ear).
- **Vertebral column 26:** cervical 7 (the first is the **atlas**, the second the **axis**), thoracic 12, lumbar 5, sacrum 1 (fused sacral vertebrae) and coccyx 1 (fused coccygeal vertebrae). A child has 33 separate vertebrae.
- **Sternum 1.**
- **Ribs 24** (12 pairs): 7 **true** pairs, 3 **false** pairs, 2 **floating** pairs.

**Appendicular skeleton (126):** **pectoral girdle 4** (clavicle and scapula on each side); **upper limbs 60** (humerus, radius, ulna, 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges, each limb); **pelvic girdle 2** (two hip bones, each of ilium, ischium and pubis fused, with the cup-shaped **acetabulum**); **lower limbs 60** (femur, tibia, fibula, patella, 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges, each limb). A hand has 27 bones and a foot 26, so both hands and both feet have 106.

**Functions:** support, protection of organs, movement (bones as levers), attachment of muscles, **blood cell formation** in red bone marrow, and storage of **calcium and phosphate** (and fat in yellow marrow).

*Note on books:* the axial skeleton is 80 only when the **hyoid and six ear ossicles** are counted in the skull (29); books that count the skull as 22 bones give a smaller axial total. The **hyoid** is the only bone that does not articulate with another bone.

Girdles and limbs: 126 bones.
The last two pairs, not attached to the sternum.

sections.heading: 4. Joints
sections.body_md:
A **joint** is the place where two or more bones meet. By structure there are three classes:
- **Fibrous joints:** the bones are joined by **dense fibrous connective tissue**; **immovable** (fixed). Example: the **sutures** between the flat bones of the skull.
- **Cartilaginous joints:** the bones are joined by **cartilage**; **slightly movable**. Examples: between the bodies of **adjacent vertebrae** and the **pubic symphysis**.
- **Synovial joints:** a **fluid-filled synovial cavity** between the bone ends; **freely movable**. The ends are covered with **articular cartilage**, the cavity is lined by the **synovial membrane**, which secretes **synovial fluid**, and a **fibrous capsule** with **ligaments** (bone to bone) holds the joint together.

**Types of synovial joint**
| Type | Movement | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Ball and socket | All directions, including rotation | Shoulder, hip |
| Hinge | One plane (bend and straighten) | Elbow, knee, finger joints |
| Pivot | Rotation about a peg | Atlas and axis (turning the head) |
| Gliding | Sliding of flat surfaces | Between carpals; between tarsals |
| Saddle | Two planes at right angles | Base of the thumb (carpometacarpal) |

*Note on books:* the knee is treated as a hinge in most school books, though it also allows a little rotation; the wrist between radius and carpals is called an ellipsoid (condyloid) joint in some books and is left out of the five-type list in others.

sections.heading: 5. Disorders of muscles and bones
sections.body_md:
| Disorder | Cause | Main symptom |
|---|---|---|
| **Myasthenia gravis** | Autoimmune: antibodies block **acetylcholine receptors** at the neuromuscular junction | Muscle weakness and fatigue; drooping eyelids, difficulty in swallowing |
| **Tetany** | **Low calcium** ions in the body fluid (for example, fall in parathormone) | Rapid, painful **spasms** of muscles |
| **Muscular dystrophy** | **Genetic**; progressive degeneration of skeletal muscle (the Duchenne type is X-linked and lacks the protein dystrophin) | Progressive wasting and weakness |
| **Arthritis** | **Inflammation of joints**: wear of cartilage (osteoarthritis) or autoimmune attack on the synovial membrane (rheumatoid arthritis) | Pain, stiffness, swelling of joints |
| **Osteoporosis** | **Decreased bone mass**, common in old age and after menopause because of **low oestrogen**; low calcium intake adds to it | Brittle bones; fractures |
| **Gout** | **Uric acid crystals** deposited in joints (high uric acid level) | Sudden, severe pain and swelling, often of the big toe |

Treatment is not asked: drugs that prolong the action of acetylcholine help in myasthenia gravis, and calcium, vitamin D and exercise help to keep bone mass.

key_terms.definition_md: Autoimmune disorder at the neuromuscular junction.
Muscle spasms from low calcium.
Loss of bone mass; brittle bones.
Joint inflammation due to uric acid crystals.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying the A band shortens in contraction (it does not; the I band and H zone narrow).
- Saying the filaments themselves shorten (they slide).
- Forgetting ATP is needed to **detach** the myosin head, not to attach it; this is why rigor mortis happens.
- Mixing up the sarcomere (Z to Z) with the A band (the length of the thick filaments).
- Confusing true, false and floating ribs, or giving the wrong totals (206, 80, 126).
- Naming the knee a ball-and-socket joint (it is a hinge).
- Writing "tetany" for "tetanus": tetany is low calcium; tetanus (muscle) is a fused contraction.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: a band or protein, a bone or joint example, a disorder named from its cause, a give-a-reason.
- 2–3-mark questions: red and white fibres; the role of calcium; rigor mortis; classification of joints; bone counts.
- 5-mark questions in parts: sliding filament theory with a labelled sarcomere; skeleton with numbers; joints with examples; disorders.

cards.back_md: The unit of contraction between two Z lines.

cards.back_md: A band dark (thick filaments); I band light (thin filaments only).

cards.back_md: Middle of the A band without thin filaments.

cards.front_md: Which band does not change in contraction?
Name the proteins of the thin filament.
What do myosin heads have that makes them work?
cards.back_md: An ATPase site and an actin-binding site.

cards.front_md: Who proposed the sliding filament theory?
What does calcium bind in contraction?
What does a new ATP do to a myosin head?
Define summation.
cards.back_md: Contractions add up when a stimulus comes before relaxation is complete.

cards.front_md: Why does rigor mortis occur?
cards.back_md: No ATP after death, so myosin heads stay attached to actin.

cards.front_md: How many bones are in the adult skeleton?
Components of the axial skeleton?
Bones of the skull count (with ossicles and hyoid)?
Adult vertebral regions?

cards.back_md: The last two pairs; not joined to the sternum.

Three classes of joint?
Example of each synovial type?
cards.back_md: Ball and socket: hip; hinge: elbow; pivot: atlas and axis; gliding: carpals; saddle: thumb base.

Cause of tetany?

questions.stem_md: In a classic demonstration, fine carbon powder is dusted on the moist roof of a frog’s mouth and slowly drifts towards the gullet. The drift is caused by

options.text_md: coordinated beating of cilia on the lining cells
contraction of striated muscle in the roof of the mouth
the lashing of a single flagellum on each cell

questions.solution_md: A moving cover of cilia, all beating in one direction, sweeps particles along — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A drop of pond water under a microscope shows green *Euglena* swimming towards the lighted side of the slide. Which structure propels it?

options.text_md: A fringe of short cilia all over the body

questions.solution_md: *Euglena* swims by a flagellum, as a sperm does — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A butcher notices that the leg of a domestic hen is dark while its breast meat is pale. The dark colour of the leg muscle shows that its fibres have

options.text_md: more sarcoplasmic reticulum and make lactic acid by glycolysis
more myoglobin and mitochondria, and rely on aerobic respiration

questions.solution_md: Red fibres are rich in myoglobin and mitochondria and make ATP aerobically — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A strip of relaxed muscle lengthens when a small weight is hung from it, and returns to its original length when the weight is removed. The two properties shown are, in order,
questions.solution_md: Stretching shows extensibility; recoil shows elasticity — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A histology slide shows long, branched fibres with cross-striations, joined end to end at dark lines, from the wall of an organ that beats without any conscious control. The tissue is
questions.solution_md: Branched, striated, involuntary fibres joined end to end: cardiac muscle — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A pathologist examining the wall of the small intestine finds spindle-shaped cells with a single nucleus each and no cross-striations. This muscle is
questions.solution_md: Unstriated, uninucleate, involuntary fibres: smooth (visceral) muscle — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The oxygen-storing pigment that gives red muscle fibres their colour is ______.
questions.solution_md: Myoglobin.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Cardiac muscle fibres are striated and are under voluntary control.
questions.solution_md: False. Cardiac muscle is striated but involuntary.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Red muscle fibres can work for a long time without tiring.

**Reason (R):** White muscle fibres contain less myoglobin than red muscle fibres.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the low myoglobin of white fibres does not explain why red fibres resist fatigue (their aerobic ATP supply does) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: State two differences between red and white skeletal muscle fibres, and name one place where white fibres are abundant.

answer.model_answer_md: **Red fibres** have much **myoglobin** and many **mitochondria**, respire **aerobically** and contract slowly without tiring; **white fibres** have little myoglobin and few mitochondria, use **anaerobic glycolysis** (forming **lactic acid**) and contract quickly but tire soon. White fibres are abundant in the **breast muscle of a domestic hen** and in the **muscles of the eyeball**.

questions.solution_md: Two differences; one place.

marking_scheme.step: Two differences between red and white fibres

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: A diving seal can stay under water for a long time even though its muscles keep working.

answer.model_answer_md: Its red muscle fibres hold a large store of **oxygen bound to myoglobin**, so they keep respiring **aerobically** while the seal is not breathing.

questions.solution_md: Myoglobin oxygen store.

marking_scheme.step: Myoglobin stores oxygen for aerobic respiration

questions.stem_md: Complete the analogy: Lining of the windpipe : ciliary movement :: swimming sperm : ______.

answer.model_answer_md: **Flagellar movement.**

questions.solution_md: Flagellum.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish ciliary, flagellar and muscular movement by the structure responsible, and give one human example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Ciliary movement** is produced by many short **cilia** beating in step, as in the **windpipe lining** that clears mucus and dust. **Flagellar movement** is produced by a single long **flagellum**, as in the **sperm**. **Muscular movement** is produced by **contraction of muscle fibres** pulling on bones or organ walls, as in **walking** or the **heartbeat**.

questions.solution_md: Three types with structures and examples.

questions.stem_md: A domestic hen can walk and scratch the ground all day but flies only in short bursts before tiring. Relate this to the kinds of muscle fibre in its legs and breast.

answer.model_answer_md: The **leg muscles** are mostly **red fibres**, rich in **myoglobin** and **mitochondria**, which make ATP **aerobically** and so work for long periods without fatigue. The **breast muscles** are mostly **white fibres**, with few mitochondria, which depend on **anaerobic glycolysis**: they contract fast and strongly but **tire quickly** as **lactic acid** builds up, so the hen flies only briefly.

questions.solution_md: Legs red; breast white; reason.

marking_scheme.step: Link to walking all day and brief flight

questions.solution_md: D is the gap between the ends of the thin filaments: the H zone — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A researcher treats isolated muscle fibres with a chemical that prevents calcium ions from binding to troponin, and then stimulates the nerve normally. What will she observe?

options.text_md: No contraction, because the sarcolemma cannot depolarise
Contraction, because myosin heads bind actin anyway
No contraction, because tropomyosin continues to cover the myosin-binding sites on actin
Rigor, because the heads cannot release ATP

questions.solution_md: Without calcium on troponin, tropomyosin stays over the binding sites, so no cross bridges form — option (c).

questions.stem_md: During one cycle of contraction, a fresh ATP molecule binds to a myosin head that has just completed its power stroke. The immediate result is that the head

options.text_md: lets go of the actin filament

answer.model_answer_md: **Arthritis** is **inflammation of the joints**, with pain, stiffness and swelling. A joint may be damaged by **wearing away of the articular cartilage** (osteoarthritis) or by an **autoimmune attack on the synovial membrane** (rheumatoid arthritis).

questions.solution_md: Inflammation; two causes.

questions.stem_md: Name the disorder in each case and give its cause: (i) a boy whose leg muscles have wasted slowly since early childhood, with other boys in his mother’s family affected; (ii) a woman whose eyelids droop and who cannot chew for long; (iii) a man with sudden severe pain in the big toe.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) **Muscular dystrophy**: a **genetic** disorder (Duchenne type is **X-linked**) with progressive degeneration of skeletal muscle. (ii) **Myasthenia gravis**: **antibodies attack acetylcholine receptors** at the neuromuscular junction, so signals fail and muscles tire. (iii) **Gout**: **uric acid crystals** deposit in the joint and cause inflammation.

questions.solution_md: Three disorders and causes.

questions.stem_md: Explain why women are more at risk of osteoporosis after menopause, and state two measures that help to prevent it.

answer.model_answer_md: **Osteoporosis** is a **decrease in bone mass** that makes bones brittle. After **menopause** the level of **oestrogen** falls, and with it the protection of bone, so bone mass is lost faster. It can be reduced by a diet rich in **calcium and vitamin D** and by regular **weight-bearing exercise**, started early in life.

questions.solution_md: Oestrogen fall; two preventions.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name the muscle disorder that results from the action of antibodies on the neuromuscular junction, and state two symptoms. [2]
(b) Differentiate between tetany and muscular dystrophy. [2]
(c) Name the disorder caused by a high level of uric acid in the blood. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Myasthenia gravis**: antibodies block **acetylcholine receptors**; symptoms are **muscle weakness and fatigue** and **drooping eyelids**.

(b) **Tetany** is caused by **low calcium** in body fluids and gives rapid **spasms**, which can be relieved when calcium is restored; **muscular dystrophy** is **genetic**, with **progressive degeneration** of muscle that is not reversed.

(c) **Gout**, in which **uric acid crystals** collect in joints.

questions.solution_md: Myasthenia gravis; tetany vs dystrophy; gout.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: Older people often break a bone after a minor fall.

answer.model_answer_md: Their **bone mass has decreased** (osteoporosis), so the bones are **thin and brittle** and break easily.

questions.solution_md: Reduced bone mass.
